entities.summary:
Charlotte Guillard was a pioneering female printer who directed the Soleil d'Or printing house in Paris during the early 16th century. Born into a time of great cultural and intellectual transformation, Guillard's innovative work played a significant role in disseminating theological texts and shaping the intellectual landscape of Western Europe.

 Operating her own publishing imprint twice during her periods of widowhood, Guillard produced a substantial body of work that showcased her expertise as a printer and publisher. Her contributions to the spread of knowledge during this period were instrumental in laying the groundwork for future generations of scholars and thinkers.

 Despite facing numerous challenges and obstacles as a woman in a male-dominated industry, Guillard persevered and left an indelible mark on the world of printing and publishing. Her legacy serves as a testament to her determination and innovative spirit.

 The exact date of Charlotte Guillard's birth is unknown, but it is believed that she was born in France around 1500.

"significanceCategory": "regional"}, "summary": "Charlotte Guillard (c. 1485–1557) was the first and most significant female master printer in France — a woman who operated one of the most prestigious printing houses in Paris for over three decades and who independently managed a commercially and intellectually elite publishing enterprise at a time when women were legally barred from most trades. She ran the Soleil d'Or (Golden Sun) printing house in the Rue Saint-Jacques — the heart of Paris's book trade — first as the widow of her first husband Berthold Rembolt, then after 1519 as the independent proprietor, and finally in partnership with her second husband Claude Chevallon. After Chevallon's death in 1537, she ran the press alone for the final twenty years of her active career, producing some of the finest scholarly typography of 16th-century France.

Guillard's press specialised in the high-end scholarly market: patristic texts, Greek and Latin classics, legal works, and theological commentaries. Her editions of the Church Fathers — Origen, Cyprian, Tertullian, John Chrysostom — were produced to the highest typographic and editorial standards, using quality paper, elegant typefaces, and scholarly apparatus. Her press printed for the Collège de France and worked with leading humanist scholars of the Paris establishment, including Guillaume Budé. At a moment when France was navigating the turbulence of the early Reformation, Guillard's patristic programme aligned her with the Erasmian reform current — a scholarly Catholicism that sought renewal through textual scholarship rather than Lutheran rupture.

The historical recovery of Charlotte Guillard's career in the 20th century transformed the history of early printing: she demonstrated that women were not merely passive inheritors of husbands' print shops but active, commercially sophisticated operators who shaped the intellectual programme of their presses.
